```{r setup}
library(eivfin)
```

## Attenuation bias in beta estimation

Consider a single-index return model: the excess return of an asset is

$$r_i = \alpha + \beta \xi_i + \varepsilon_i,$$

where $\xi_i$ is the (unobserved) systematic factor. In practice the factor
is proxied by a measured quantity $m_i = \xi_i + \eta_i$ -- an index that
imperfectly tracks the true market portfolio, as in Roll's (1977) critique.
Ordinary least squares of $r_i$ on $m_i$ then produces an attenuated slope,
biased toward zero by the reliability factor
$\sigma_\xi^2 / (\sigma_\xi^2 + \sigma_\eta^2)$.

We simulate a market factor with monthly standard deviation of 4% and a
proxy observed with a 1% measurement error:

```{r simulation}
set.seed(2024)
n <- 240
beta_true <- 1.2
xi <- rnorm(n, sd = 0.04)
r  <- 0.005 + beta_true * xi + rnorm(n, sd = 0.01)
m  <- xi + rnorm(n, sd = 0.01)

ols_beta <- cov(m, r) / var(m)
ols_beta
```

The attenuation factor is `0.04^2 / (0.04^2 + 0.01^2) = 0.941`, so OLS is
expected near `1.2 * 0.941 = 1.13`. Both measurement errors here have
equal variance (1% each), so orthogonal regression (total least squares)
is the appropriate EIV estimator; with `lambda = 1`, Deming regression is
the same estimator and serves as a cross-check:

```{r estimates}
fit_tls <- tls(m, r, B = 500, seed = 2024)
fit_dem <- deming(m, r, lambda = 1, se = "jackknife")

data.frame(
  truth  = beta_true,
  OLS    = ols_beta,
  TLS    = unname(coef(fit_tls)[2]),
  Deming = unname(coef(fit_dem)[2])
)
```

Both EIV estimators remove essentially all of the attenuation bias, while
OLS understates the beta by roughly 6%.

```{r plot}
plot(m, r, pch = 19, cex = 0.6,
     xlab = "observed factor proxy", ylab = "excess return")
abline(a = 0.005, b = beta_true, lty = 2)
abline(a = coef(fit_tls)[1], b = coef(fit_tls)[2], col = "red")
legend("topleft", lty = c(2, 1), col = c("black", "red"),
       legend = c("true relation", "TLS fit"), bty = "n")
```

## Unequal error variances: Deming regression

When the two error variances differ, TLS is inconsistent and the Deming
estimator with the known ratio
$\lambda = \sigma_{e_y}^2 / \sigma_{e_x}^2$ should be used instead. Here
the return equation noise is 2% while the proxy error stays at 1%, so
$\lambda = 4$:

```{r unequal}
set.seed(2025)
r2 <- 0.005 + beta_true * xi + rnorm(n, sd = 0.02)
m2 <- xi + rnorm(n, sd = 0.01)

fit_dem2 <- deming(m2, r2, lambda = 4, se = "jackknife")
data.frame(
  truth  = beta_true,
  OLS    = cov(m2, r2) / var(m2),
  Deming = unname(coef(fit_dem2)[2])
)
confint(fit_dem2)
```

The Deming estimator with the correct ratio is again close to the true
beta, while OLS is attenuated by the larger reliability factor
`0.04^2 / (0.04^2 + 0.01^2 + 0.02^2)`.

## Notes and references

- Fuller, W. A. (1987). *Measurement Error Models*. Wiley.
- Roll, R. (1977). A critique of the asset pricing theory's tests.
  *Journal of Financial Economics*, 4(2), 129-176.
- Carroll, R. J., Ruppert, D., Stefanski, L. A. and Crainiceanu, C. M.
  (2006). *Measurement Error in Nonlinear Models*, 2nd ed. Chapman & Hall.
